title: Eight rungs of giving (Matanot Aniyim 10)
hookLine: from giving grudgingly up to making someone self-sufficient
last: NO ONE IS EXCUSED FROM TORAH STUDY.

cards: Someone asks for help, and you give. Fine. But how?
With a sigh, eyes on your phone, handing over less than you could? Before they even had to ask? Or in a way that means they'll never need to ask again?

Maimonides, in his laws of gifts to the poor, says giving isn't one act. It's a ladder: there are eight levels in giving, he says, each one higher than the one below. You met this ladder in your first weeks on the path.

teach.b: Eight rungs of giving. Climb from the bottom. Lowest: giving grudgingly, with a sour face.
Still giving. Still a rung. Next: giving less than you should, but gladly.
Then: giving the right amount, but only after being asked. Then: giving before being asked, straight into the person's hand. So far, both people know each other.
Now the ladder turns to who knows what. Next: the poor person knows who gave, but the giver doesn't know who received.

Some sages, Maimonides says, tied coins into the backs of their cloaks, and the poor came and took them. Higher: the giver knows, the receiver doesn't. Some sages slipped coins secretly through a poor person's door.
Higher still: neither knows the other.
And at the very top: strengthening a person before they fall, with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask anyone.
The next two days climb those top rungs slowly.
Notice the shape. The bottom rungs are about the giver's heart, the middle about the receiver's dignity, the top about the receiver's future. And even the lowest rung is on the ladder.
The point isn't to shame anyone at the bottom.

teach.h: EACH RUNG HIGHER THAN THE LAST.
teach.b: It's to show there's always one rung higher. This week walked from the foundation of foundations, through love and awe, the body, the doctor and the student, to the open hand. Knowledge first, and then it turns outward.

how: Maimonides' ladder of tzedakah is taught in Jewish schools and synagogues as a guide to how to give, not only how much.

games.q: what does “eight rungs of giving” mean?
o: a ladder of giving, from grudging gift to self-reliance
eight nights of gifts given during Hanukkah
eight steps up to the Temple's inner courtyard

games.q: the eight rungs — tap the pairs.
p: the receiver knows, the giver doesn't
a gift, loan, partnership or job

s: Maimonides says a grudging gift doesn't count
it's the lowest rung, but it's on the ladder.
giving before being asked is higher than giving after
giving into someone's hand before they ask is a rung above giving after the request.
the top rung is giving the largest amount
the top rung is strengthening someone, with a gift, loan, partnership or job, so they won't need to ask.

games.q: you're a sage. you want to give to the poor, but you don't want to see their faces as they take it. what do you do?
o: hand it to them and look away.
tie coins into the back of your cloak and let them take.
stop giving until you can do it better.
games.why: Maimonides says some sages tied coins behind them in their cloaks. the poor knew who gave; the giver didn't know who took.

practice: Bring to mind the last time you gave something, money, time, a favor, and ask honestly, and kindly, which rung it was on.
Then picture the same gift one rung up: given more gladly, or before being asked, or more quietly, so the other person keeps their dignity.

wordCard.voice: Eight rungs of giving. Maimonides' ladder of tzedakah, from the grudging gift at the bottom to helping someone stand on their own at the top. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: eight levels, Maimonides' phrase for the rungs of tzedakah in Matanot Aniyim 10:7.

carryVoice: Your line: the eight rungs. Wherever you stand, there's one rung higher. A full week of Maimonides, done.
